column2: Synchronised multi-transmitter spoofing of multilateration
column4:
1. Time-synchronised SDR transmitters send forged ADS-B
2. Timing errors look like one genuine emitter, so TDOA checks pass
3. Ghost aircraft is located within 5 s
4. A real track is diverted by 15 degrees and its verification flag removed
column8: Terrestrial MLAT, not LEO. Reaching the ATM picture is not shown.

column2: Satellite downlink overshadowing
column4:
1. Attacker transmits over a satellite downlink near the ground station
2. Ground side accepts the attacker's data
3. Spoofed Earth-observation data accepted by a lab copy of a ground decoder
column7:
Salkield et al. (2023)

column8: Not an MLAT payload. Second result used a lab replica.

column2: Time-protocol attack shifts client clocks
column4:
1. On-path or off-path attacker acts on the NTP/PTP exchange
2. Client time is shifted or synchronisation denied
3. Delay attacks work even with cryptographic protection
column7:
Malhotra, Cohen, Brakke & Goldberg (2016)
https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/attacking-network-time-protocol.pdf
Ullmann & Vögeler (2009)
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5340224
column8: Spread to the L1 clocks is the atlas assessment. Ullmann is theoretical (E0).

column2: Viasat KA-SAT management-network intrusion
column4:
1. Intruder enters the management network through a misconfigured VPN
2. Destructive commands are sent to user terminals
3. Tens of thousands of modems go offline
column8: The satellite was not affected. Terminals, not a surveillance payload.

column2: Mission-control and flight-software exploitation
column4:
1. Remote code execution on ground command-and-control software
2. Flight software and the SDLS library also carry CVEs
3. Stated aim: disrupt or seize a mission
column8: Conference talk, 45 CVEs. No end-to-end attack on a live mission is recorded.

column2: GPS ground-segment error shifts broadcast time
column4:
1. Ground software flaw triggers when SVN 23 is removed
2. Broadcast UTC shifts by about 13 microseconds for hours
3. Receivers using the broadcast time inherit the offset
column7:
US Air Force, via RNT Foundation (2016)
https://rntfnd.org/?p=4536
column8: A fault, not an attack. Shows the timing dependency failing top-down.

column2: Galileo ground-segment malfunction, July 2019
column4:
1. Equipment malfunction in the ground segment
2. Navigation-message updates stop
3. Navigation and timing interrupted for six days
column8: A fault, not an attack.

column2: GNSS interference degrades aircraft surveillance
column4:
1. Wide-area GNSS jamming or spoofing
2. Aircraft navigation and ADS-B surveillance degrade
3. Flights diverted and a route suspended (Helsinki-Tartu)

column2: Satellite ADS-C: passive collection, then injection
column4:
1. Over 120,000 live ADS-C messages collected passively
2. Lab tests show downlink and uplink injection and contract manipulation
column8: Two separate results, not one attack run. Injection shown in the lab only.

column2: SATCOM terminal firmware to remote compromise
column4:
1. Backdoors and hard-coded credentials in terminal firmware (2014)
2. In-service terminals reported remotely reachable and exploitable (2018)
column8: Two talks four years apart, not one chain.

column2: Exploit delivered over an unauthenticated data link
column4:
1. Exploit sent over an unauthenticated data link
2. On-board flight software compromised (simulated systems)
column8: Lab simulation only (E1).

column2: Spoofed time and false data degrade estimation
column4:
1. Spoofed GPS time corrupts PMU phase measurements; fault detection degrades
2. Stealthy false-data injection bypasses residual-based detection
column7:
Zhang et al. (2013)
https://doi.org/10.1109/TSG.2012.2227342
Liu, Ning & Reiter (2009; extended 2011)
https://doi.org/10.1145/1653662.1653666
column8: Power-grid analogue, not air traffic.

column2: Ghost aircraft and jamming against real ADS-B receivers
column4:
1. Forged 1090ES messages are generated with commodity SDR equipment
2. Real ADS-B receivers accept them and show ghost aircraft
3. The same equipment can also jam reception
column7:
Costin & Francillon (2012)
https://www.eurecom.fr/publication/3788
Schäfer, Lenders & Martinovic (2013)
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-38980-1_16
column8: Ground receivers, not the LEO payload. Atlas note: would reach L3 association if not filtered. Costin is a talk (not peer-reviewed).

column2: Satellite takeover through firmware flaws and unprotected telecommand
column4:
1. Firmware of three real satellites is analysed
2. Exploitable on-board firmware flaws are found
3. Telecommand is left unprotected, so the flaws can be reached
4. Takeover of the satellite is shown on emulated systems
column8: Emulation, no live satellite attacked (E1).

column2: Secure-boot bypass by fault injection on a satellite user terminal
column4:
1. Voltage fault injection on a real Starlink user terminal
2. Secure boot is bypassed
3. Root access is gained on the researcher's own device
column8: User terminal, not a satellite or payload. Conference talk (not peer-reviewed).

column2: Link flooding that exploits the predictable LEO topology
column4:
1. The attacker uses the predictable LEO topology
2. Bottleneck links are chosen as targets
3. Cheap flooding congests them (Starlink-like constellation simulations)
column8: Simulation only (E1). Sources #16 and #21 of the atlas give platforms to repeat such experiments; they add no attack.

column2: GNSS receiver capture, then defeat of navigation-message authentication
column4:
1. A portable spoofer tracks the live GNSS signals
2. It smoothly captures the target receiver; simple consistency checks fail to detect it (2008)
3. If the receiver uses OSNMA, manipulating its time synchronisation lets the spoofed signals through (2025)
column7:
Humphreys et al. (2008)
https://www.ion.org/publications/abstract.cfm?articleID=8132
Wang et al. (2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09246
column8: Two results 17 years apart, not one run. Wang 2025 is a preprint (controlled setting, commercial receiver and SDRs). Atlas note: threatens any GNSS-disciplined clock in the sync chain.

column2: GNSS spoofing of aircraft seen in space-based ADS-B data
column4:
1. The GNSS position source of aircraft is spoofed
2. The spoofing is visible in operational space-based ADS-B data
column8: Industry white paper (E3). At the 13 Oct 2026 check the page could not be fetched; only its title matched.

column2: GNSS spoofing displaces vessel positions in AIS
column4:
1. GNSS spoofing displaces the positions vessels report
2. 9,883 suspected instances affecting 1,311 vessels since February 2016 are found in public AIS data and with an ISS-mounted sensor
column8: Not bound to a catalogue threat in the atlas; listed under T1.03 as the closest threat because AIS plays the role of ADS-B.

column2: Overshadowing of ILS guidance signals
column4:
1. Spoofed ILS signals are sent from COTS SDRs
2. They control aviation-grade receivers in real time
3. Simulated autoland runs end with offset touchdowns
column8: Aircraft landing guidance, not surveillance. Bound to T1.07 in the atlas.
